p.src: Now Song Jiang commanded his troops and divided them into five columns, which advanced upon Gaizhou. Gaizhou's scouts learned the truth of the matter and sped back to report it within the city. The commander defending the city, Niu Wenzhong, had begun his career among the outlaws of the greenwood. He had given all the gold, silver, and valuables he robbed upon the rivers and lakes to support Tian Hu, conspired with him in rebellion, and seized prefectures and counties of the Song realm; for this he had been appointed Military Affairs Commissioner. He was accustomed to wielding a three-pointed, double-edged blade, and his martial skill was outstanding. Under his command were four fierce generals known as the Four Generals of Might, who joined him in guarding Gaizhou. Who were these four? Fang Qiong, the Lion-Might General; An Shirong, the Pixiu-Might General; Chu Heng, the Leopard-Might General; and Yu Yulin, the Bear-Might General.

p.src: Each of the Four Generals of Might had four subordinate commanders under him, making sixteen subordinate commanders in all. They were Yang Duan, Guo Xin, Su Ji, Zhang Xiang, Fang Shun, Shen An, Lu Yuan, Wang Ji, Shi Jing, Qin Sheng, Mo Zhen, Sheng Ben, He Ren, Cao Hong, Shi Xun, and Sang Ying.

p.src: Together with his senior and subordinate officers, Niu Wenzhong commanded thirty thousand northern troops and held Gaizhou. Having lately heard that Lingchuan and Gaoping had fallen, he prepared to meet the imperial army while sending urgent dispatches to Weisheng and Jinning to request reinforcements. Upon receiving the report, he immediately sent the senior general Fang Qiong and the subordinate commanders Yang Duan, Guo Xin, Su Ji, and Zhang Xiang out of the city with five thousand troops to meet the enemy. As they departed, Niu Wenzhong said, “Take care, General. I shall follow with troops to support you.” Fang Qiong replied, “There is no need for Your Excellency to remind me. Those two cities fell not because their strength was unequal to the foe, but because both were caught by his trickery. If I do not kill several of them today, I swear I shall not return to the city.”

p.src: They all donned their armor, mounted their horses, and led the troops out through the eastern gate, charging toward the enemy. The Song vanguard met them, drew up in battle formation, and beat its drums until the heavens resounded. When the gate banner in the northern ranks opened, Fang Qiong rode forth, flanked on either side by four subordinate commanders. Fang Qiong wore a cloud-scroll crown upon his head, dragon-scale armor over a green brocade robe, a lion-patterned belt about his waist, and green-trimmed boots upon his feet. A bow hung on his left and arrows on his right; astride a yellow-maned horse and gripping a solid-iron spear, he shouted, “You bandits of the marshes! How dare you seize our cities by deceit!” From the Song ranks, Sun Li shouted, “Rebel who aids a traitor! Heaven's army has arrived, yet you still do not know that death is upon you!” He spurred his horse and charged straight at Fang Qiong. Amid clouds of battle dust and a thicket of murderous fury, the two generals fought for more than thirty bouts, until Fang Qiong's strength gradually began to fail. In the northern ranks, Zhang Xiang saw that Fang Qiong could not prevail against Sun Li. He took up his bow, nocked an arrow, edged his horse out before the lines, and loosed it at Sun Li with a hiss. Sun Li had already spotted him and jerked up his horse's head; the arrow struck the horse squarely in the eye, and it reared upright. Sun Li leapt aside, gripped his spear, and continued the fight on foot. Maddened by pain, the horse ran a dozen or more paces toward the north before collapsing. Seeing that his arrow had failed to bring Sun Li down, Zhang Xiang galloped forward with saber raised to join the fight, but Qin Ming intercepted him and engaged him in combat. Sun Li wished to return to the ranks and change horses, but Fang Qiong's spear pressed him relentlessly on every side, entangling him so that he could not escape. This enraged Hua Rong, the Divine-Armed General, who cursed, “How dare that rebel general shoot a hidden arrow! Let him taste one of mine!” Even as he spoke, he had drawn his bow to the full. Taking careful aim at Fang Qiong from close range, he loosed a single hissing arrow that struck Fang Qiong squarely in the face and sent him tumbling from his horse. Sun Li rushed up and finished him with one thrust of his spear, then hurried back to his own lines to change horses. As Zhang Xiang fought Qin Ming, Qin Ming's club never strayed from above Zhang Xiang's head, and Zhang Xiang could do no more than parry and fend it off. When he also saw Fang Qiong fall from his horse, fear entered his heart, and he gradually began to lose ground. From the northern ranks, Guo Xin spurred his horse and came with spear in hand to aid Zhang Xiang. Qin Ming faced both generals without the slightest fear. The three horses spread into a T-shaped formation as they fought before the lines. Hua Rong took a second arrow, set it to the string, and carefully sighted upon Zhang Xiang's back. Drawing his bow into a full moon, he sent the arrow flying like a meteor and shouted, “Take my arrow!” It struck Zhang Xiang squarely in the back and pierced him clean through, the arrowhead emerging from his chest. His helmet hung awry, his feet kicked empty air, and he crashed from his horse with a thud. Seeing Zhang Xiang struck by the arrow, Guo Xin feigned an opening, wheeled his horse, and fled toward his own ranks, with Qin Ming in close pursuit. By then Sun Li had changed horses and ridden back out. Together with Hua Rong and Suo Chao, he rallied the troops and swept forward in a charge, throwing the northern army into chaos. Yang Duan, Guo Xin, and Su Ji could no longer withstand them and hastily retreated. Suddenly tremendous shouting arose behind the northern troops. Fearing that Fang Qiong might meet with disaster, Niu Wenzhong had ordered An Shirong and Yu Yulin each to lead five thousand men and close in from two directions. Hua Rong and the other three generals hurriedly divided their troops to resist them, but Yang Duan, Guo Xin, and Su Ji reined their forces around and attacked again. Unable to withstand an attack from three sides, Hua Rong and the other three generals fought desperately to break through, but were on the verge of being trapped at the heart of the encirclement. Then battle cries rose to the heavens in the east, and the northern army fell into disorder. Dong Ping and six other generals came on from the left, Huang Xin and six others from the right; the troops on both wings charged forward together, routing the northern army and killing great numbers. An Shirong, Yu Yulin, and the others hurriedly crowded back into the city with their troops and shut the gates. The Song troops pursued them to the foot of the walls, but beams and stone projectiles came crashing down from above, forcing them at last to withdraw.

p.src: Before long, Vanguard Song and the entire army arrived and made camp five li from the city. Song Jiang took his seat in the command tent and ordered Xiao Rang to record Hua Rong's foremost merit. Suddenly, a strange wind arose, whirling dust and earth from west to east and shaking all the banners askew. Wu Yong said, “This wind portends that the enemy will raid our camp tonight. We must make ready at once.” Song Jiang said, “This wind is indeed no ordinary one!” He ordered Ou Peng, Deng Fei, Yan Shun, and Ma Lin to take three thousand men and lie in ambush to the left of the camp, while Wang Ying, Chen Da, Yang Chun, and Li Zhong took three thousand men to ambush on its right; Lu Zhishen, Wu Song, Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun were to lead five hundred men in ambush within the camp and, at the signal of a cannon shot, charge out together. When all had been assigned, Song Jiang and Wu Yong discussed military affairs by candlelight. Now Niu Wenzhong, having lost three generals, mustered his troops and found that more than two thousand men were gone. As he sat brooding in his tent, An Shirong, the “Mighty General,” offered a plan: “Set your mind at ease, my lord! Song Jiang's band has won several battles in succession and is now swollen with pride. They will surely be unprepared. Tonight I shall lead a force to raid their camp. We can win a complete victory and avenge today's defeat.” Privy Councillor Niu said, “If you go, General, I shall personally lead troops in support. I shall order Generals Yu and Chu to hold the city securely.” An Shirong rejoiced. “If Your Excellency takes the field in person, Song Jiang will surely be captured.” Their plan settled, at the second watch Shirong and the subordinate generals Shen An, Lu Yuan, Wang Ji, and Shi Jing led five thousand troops out of the city. The men wore light armor, the horses' bells had been removed, and the soldiers hurried silently with gags in their mouths. Reaching Song's camp, they raised a battle cry and surged in to attack. But the camp gate stood wide open and the whole enclosure blazed with lamps and candles. Realizing he had fallen into a trap, An Shirong hastily retreated. A cannon boomed inside Song's camp. From the left Yan Shun and three other generals, and from the right Wang Ying and three others, charged in together. From within the camp, Li Kui and the other five generals led shield-bearing infantry in a rolling charge outside. The northern army was routed and scattered in every direction to save their lives. Shen An was cut down by a single stroke of Wu Song's戒刀, and Wang Ji was slain by Wang Ying. Song's troops surrounded the forces of An Shirong, Lu Yuan, and Shi Jing at the heart of the battlefield. Just as their peril became extreme, Niu Wenzhong arrived with the subordinate generals Cao Hong and Shi Xun and rescued them. After a confused melee, both sides withdrew their troops.

p.src: The next day, Niu Wenzhong mustered his troops and found that more than a thousand had been lost. He had also lost the two generals Shen An and Wang Ji. Shi Xun was gravely wounded and barely clinging to life. While Niu was sunk in anxiety, it was suddenly reported that an envoy had arrived from Weisheng bearing a decree. Niu Wenzhong hurriedly mounted and rode out through the north gate to receive him. The envoy entered the city and read the decree aloud. It said that the Directorate of Astronomy, observing the heavens by night, had lately seen a Star of the Dipper invade the celestial region corresponding to Jin; the city must therefore be held firmly without the slightest failure. Niu Wenzhong reported that the Song court had sent Song Jiang and his forces to attack them and that two cities had already fallen in succession. Song's troops had now reached this place, and in yesterday's fighting five chief and subordinate officers had been lost. Only if reinforcements arrived soon could the city be kept safe. The envoy said, “When I left Weisheng, no such news had yet arrived. Only when I was halfway here did I begin to hear reports that the Song court had sent troops into our territory.” Niu Wenzhong gave a banquet for the envoy and presented him with gifts. Meanwhile, he prepared rolling logs and stones, powerful bows and crossbows, fire arrows and incendiary weapons, and held the city firmly while awaiting reinforcements. Of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Now Yan Shun, Wang Ying, and the other generals, having scattered the enemy who raided the camp, returned victorious. The next day, Song Jiang ordered siege carts and other equipment repaired in preparation for an assault. Lin Chong, Suo Chao, Xuan Zan, and Hao Siwen were to lead ten thousand men against the east gate; Xu Ning, Qin Ming, Han Tao, and Peng Qi were to lead ten thousand men against the south gate; Dong Ping, Yang Zhi, Shan Tinggui, and Wei Dingguo were to lead ten thousand men against the west gate. The north gate was left open, lest reinforcements arrive and the defenders sally out, catching Song's army between two forces. Shi Jin, Zhu Tong, Mu Hong, and Ma Lin were ordered to lead five thousand men in ambush below the high ridge northeast of the city; Huang Xin, Sun Li, Ou Peng, and Deng Fei were to take five thousand men and lie in ambush in the dense woods northwest of the city. Should the enemy summon reinforcements, the two forces were to attack from both sides. Hua Rong, Wang Ying, Zhang Qing, Sun Xin, and Li Li were ordered to lead one thousand cavalry as roving scouts, patrolling the four gates for intelligence; Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, Li Gun, Liu Tang, and Lei Heng were to lead three hundred infantry and support Hua Rong's force. Once the assignments were settled, all the generals departed in obedience to their orders. Song Jiang, Lu Junyi, Wu Yong, and the other chief and subordinate officers moved their camp to a point one li east of the city. Li Yun and Tang Long were ordered to oversee repairs to the scaling ladders and siege towers and have them pushed to the various camps for use.

p.src: At the eastern wall, Lin Chong and the other three generals erected scaling ladders and siege towers and pushed them close to the ramparts. They ordered agile soldiers to climb the towers and scramble toward the wall while the men below shouted encouragement. But fire arrows flew from within the city like a swarm of locusts, and the soldiers could not dodge them fast enough. In no time the siege tower was burned through and came crashing down with a great clatter. Five or six soldiers fell to their deaths, and more than ten were wounded. The assaults on the west and south sides likewise cost soldiers to fire arrows and cannon fire. Thus, even after six or seven consecutive days of assault, the city could not be taken.

p.src: Seeing that the city could not be taken, Song Jiang went in person with Lu Junyi and Wu Yong beneath the south gate to press the assault. There they saw Hua Rong and the other four generals leading the roving cavalry eastward from a scouting patrol in the west. On the gate tower, Yu Yulin and the subordinate generals Yang Duan and Guo Xin were overseeing the defending troops. When Yang Duan saw Hua Rong drawing near the tower, he said, “The other day he wounded two of our generals in succession. Today I shall avenge them!” He hastily raised his bow, set an arrow to the string, and shot it whistling straight at Hua Rong's chest. Hearing the bowstring twang, Hua Rong leaned backward just as the arrow arrived. With one easy sweep of his hand he caught it and clenched it between his teeth; straightening up, he secured his spear in its saddle ring, took his bow in his left hand, and with his right retrieved that same arrow. He set it to the string, took careful aim at Yang Duan, and loosed. The arrow struck Yang Duan squarely in the throat, and he toppled backward with a thud. Hua Rong shouted, “How dare you rats loose a treacherous arrow! I shall make every last one of you die!” He reached with his right hand for another arrow and was about to shoot again when a cry arose on the tower and several soldiers all tumbled down from it. Yu Yulin and Guo Xin turned ashen with terror and scrambled for cover. Hua Rong sneered, “Now you know the ‘Divine-Arrow General’!” Song Jiang and Lu Junyi cheered him without cease. Wu Yong said, “Elder brother, this is an excellent chance for us to accompany General Hua and inspect the city's defenses and terrain.” With Hua Rong and the others guarding them, Song Jiang, Lu Junyi, and Wu Yong made a complete circuit of the city and inspected it.

p.src: Song Jiang, Lu Junyi, and Wu Yong returned to the stronghold. Wu Yong summoned Geng Gong, the surrendered general from Linchuan, and questioned him about the layout of Gaizhou city. Geng Gong said, “Niu Wenzhong has made the old prefectural offices his command headquarters, in the very center of the city. There are several temples in the north of the city, while all the open ground is used as pasture.” After hearing this, Wu Yong conferred with Song Jiang, then summoned Shi Qian and Shi Xiu and whispered to them: “Proceed according to this plan. Go to Hua Rong’s army, secretly convey our orders, and act as circumstances dictate.” He next summoned Ling Zhen, Xie Zhen, and Xie Bao and ordered them to lead two hundred soldiers, taking with them large and small Thunderclap mother-and-child cannon, and proceed as instructed. He ordered Lu Zhishen and Wu Song to lead three hundred drummers and gong-men, while Liu Tang, Yang Xiong, Yu Baosi, and Duan Jingzhu each led two hundred soldiers equipped with torches; they were to go respectively east, south, west, and north and carry out the plan. He also sent Dai Zong to the eastern, western, and southern camps with secret orders: as soon as fire arose within the city, they were to join forces and storm it. When all the assignments had been made, the chieftains departed in obedience to their orders. p.src: Now the force approaching from the northwest had been sent by Tian Biao, Third Prince and brother of Tian Hu, who commanded the defenses of Jinning. On receiving Gaizhou’s plea for aid, he had dispatched his fierce subordinate, Wang Yuan of Fengxiang, with twenty thousand troops to the rescue. They had passed Yangcheng and were advancing toward Gaizhou. When they were still more than ten li from the city, a cannon suddenly sounded, and two bodies of troops burst from the dense woods beneath the high ridges to east and west. They were led by eight fierce generals—Shi Jin, Zhu Tong, Mu Hong, Ma Lin, Huang Xin, Sun Li, Ou Peng, and Deng Fei—and ten thousand stalwart soldiers swept in for the kill. Though the Jinning army numbered twenty thousand, they were exhausted by their long march. How could they withstand elite troops who had lain in ambush here for more than ten days, resting their strength, and now attacked them from both sides? The Jinning army suffered a crushing defeat, abandoning countless gongs, drums, banners, spears, helmets, armor, and horses. More than half the soldiers were killed. Wang Yuan of Fengxiang escaped with his life and led the surviving officers and troops back to Jinning; nothing more need be said of them.

p.src: To return to Niu Wenzhong: when he saw the two armies intercept and engage each other, he hurriedly sent Yu Yulin to lead troops out through the north gate in support. There were in fact no enemy troops attacking that gate. Yu Yulin led his troops out of the city, but had barely crossed the drawbridge when they encountered Hua Rong’s mounted patrol coming from the west. The northern soldiers cried out, “The Divine Archer General is here!” Panic-stricken, they fled headlong, surging back into the city in disorder. Yu Yulin had already been scared out of his wits at the southern wall. He dared not offer battle and also fled back into the city. Hua Rong and his men charged forward and killed more than twenty, but did not pursue the others, allowing them to enter the city. Those within hurriedly shut the gate.

p.src: By then, Shi Xiu and Shi Qian had put on Northern Army uniforms and slipped unnoticed into the city. Once through the gate, Shi Qian and Shi Xiu took advantage of the commotion to slip into a narrow lane. Around the bend they found a shrine whose signboard read: “Shrine of the Local Earth God.” Shi Qian and Shi Xiu slipped inside and saw a Daoist warming himself by a fire beneath the eastern wall. Seeing two soldiers enter, the Daoist asked, “Officers, what news is there outside?” One of the soldiers replied, “Just now General Yu ordered us out to fight, but we ran into the Divine Arrow General, and even General Yu dared not engage him. We all scrambled back into the city, and amid the confusion we slipped away to this place.” He took two small pieces of loose silver from his person, handed them to the Daoist, and said, “If you have any wine hidden away, bring us a couple of bowls, whatever it is. We are truly frozen through.” The man laughed and said, “Officer, you do not understand. The fighting has been so desperate these past few days that the gods have received no offerings at all. Where could I get even half a drop of wine?” He handed the silver back to Shi Qian. Shi Xiu pushed his hand back and said, “Keep this little bit for now. We can settle the rest later. We have worn ourselves out guarding the city day after day, without a moment to close our eyes. Let us sleep here tonight, and we will leave at dawn.” The Daoist waved his hands and said, “Please do not take offense, officers! General Niu’s orders are strict, and he will soon come to inspect this place. If I let you stay here, none of us will escape unscathed.” Shi Qian said, “If that is how it is, we shall find somewhere else.” Shi Xiu moved close beside the Daoist and began warming himself at the fire as well. Shi Qian looked about and, seeing no one before or behind them, gave Shi Xiu a wink. Shi Xiu stealthily drew his sword. While the Daoist remained intent on the fire, Shi Xiu struck from behind with a slicing blow and cut off his head. They then barred the shrine door. It was now around the hour of the Rooster. Shi Qian went around the divine kitchen and found a doorway in the rear wall. Beyond it lay a tiny courtyard, with two heaps of loose straw piled beneath the eaves. Shi Qian and Shi Xiu carried the straw inside and used it to cover the Daoist’s corpse. Then they opened the shrine door and climbed onto the roof from the rear courtyard. The two lay hidden below the ridge and looked up as dozens of stars appeared brightly along the horizon. After waiting for a while, Shi Qian and Shi Xiu slipped down from the roof and went outside the shrine to reconnoiter. Not a soul was passing by. They went a few steps farther and looked to either side. Though several families lived nearby, every door was tightly shut and faint sounds of weeping could be heard. Shi Qian went farther south and rounded a stretch of earthen wall. Beyond it lay a vast open ground containing dozens of stacks of firewood and fodder. Shi Qian thought, “This is the fodder yard. Why are there no soldiers guarding it?” In fact, all the officers and soldiers in the city were occupied with defending the walls and had no time to inspect this place. The guards assigned there, hearing that the Song army had routed the relief force and reckoning the city was doomed, had each thought only of saving his own life and gone into hiding beforehand. Shi Qian and Shi Xiu returned to the shrine, fetched a flame, and set fire to the straw covering the Daoist’s corpse. Then they slipped into the fodder yard, split up, and started fires in six or seven places in quick succession. Before long, fire roared through the yard and fierce flames leapt skyward; the shrine too began to burn. A resident on the west side of the yard heard that a fire had broken out and came outside with a torch to investigate. Shi Qian rushed forward and snatched the torch from his hand. Shi Xiu said, “We are going to report this to Marshal Niu.” Seeing that the two were soldiers, the resident did not dare argue with them. Torch in hand, Shi Qian ran straight south with Shi Xiu, shouting that they were going to alert the marshal. Whenever they found an easy place beneath a dwelling, they thrust the torch in and started another two fires. Then they threw the torch down and slipped away to one side.

p.src: When fires were seen rising from four or five parts of the city, the whole place erupted into an uproar. Seeing the fodder yard ablaze, Niu Wenzhong hurriedly led his troops there to fight the fire. Those outside saw the fires within the city and knew that Shi Qian and Shi Xiu had answered them from inside, so they attacked with all their strength. Song Jiang and Wu Yong led Xie Zhen and Xie Bao at a gallop to the southern wall. Wu Yong said, “The other day I noticed that the wall over there was somewhat lower.” He ordered Qin Ming and the others to push the siege towers close against the wall. Wu Yong said to Xie Zhen and Xie Bao, “The rebels have lost heart and their soldiers are exhausted. Brothers, make every effort to scale the wall!” Xie Zhen took his broad-bladed sword up the siege tower, seized the battlement, and vaulted onto the wall. Xie Bao sprang up after him. The two raised a battle cry, charged down from the battlements, and slashed wildly with their blades. The soldiers on the wall were already exhausted and terrified. Seeing how ferocious Xie Zhen and Xie Bao were, they scattered in confusion and tumbled down from the wall. When Chu Heng saw the two men atop the wall, he leveled his spear and fought them for more than ten bouts. Xie Bao felled him with a thrust of his broad-bladed sword, and Xie Zhen rushed up and hacked off his head. By then, more than a hundred Song soldiers had climbed from the siege towers onto the wall. With Xie Zhen and Xie Bao at their head, they all charged down into the city, shouting, “Anyone who comes forward will be chopped into mince!” They killed Shi Jing and Qin Sheng, cut down the soldiers guarding the gate, seized it, and lowered the drawbridge, whereupon Xu Ning and the other generals led their troops surging into the city. Xu Ning and Han Tao led troops toward the eastern gate. An Shirong could not withstand them and was stabbed to death by Xu Ning. They seized the gate and let Lin Chong and the other generals into the city. Qin Ming and Peng Qi led troops to seize the western gate and admitted Dong Ping and the others into the city. Mo Zhen, He Ren, and Cao Hong were killed amid the melee. Corpses lay strewn through the marketplaces, and blood filled the streets. Seeing that every gate had been taken, Niu Wenzhong had no choice but to mount his horse and abandon the city. Together with Yu Yulin and more than two hundred men, he fled through the northern gate. Before they had gone a single li, Black Whirlwind Li Kui and Flowery Monk Lu Zhishen suddenly emerged from the darkness—one a fierce warrior, the other a reckless monk—and barred their way. Heaven’s close-spread snare left no room to step; earth’s high-drawn net allowed no means of escape. As for what became of Niu Wenzhong and Yu Yulin, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
